Generating text¶

A post XSLT often has to write a file in some format: source code, HTML, Markdown, SQL, JSON. Writing that text with xsl:text and xsl:value-of inside the XSLT mixes two things: the logic (which aggregates, which order) and the text (the shape of a table, a class, a page). The text gets hard to read, and a change of formatting means a change of logic.

The recommended way is to keep the text in an XML template and let the XSLT fill it.

The text can be in any language or format. The examples below produce HTML and SQL, but a template for source code in any language, JSON or a configuration file works the same way. Galimatron does not know or care what is inside.

A template file¶

A template is a small XML file. Its text is copied as it is, and elements in the code namespace are marks that the XSLT fills in.

xslt/templates/page.xml (from the galimatron_hello project):

<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>
<code:template xmlns:code="galimatron-code-generation">
<html>
<head>
<title>Galimatron</title>
</head>
<body>
<p>Counter: <code:counter/></p>
<p><code:greetings/></p>
</body>
</html>
</code:template>

<code:counter/> is a hole. The XSLT knows the value and puts it there.

A template for SQL looks the same:

<code:template xmlns:code="galimatron-code-generation">
CREATE TABLE <code:table-name/> (
<code:columns/>);
<code:when-checked>ALTER TABLE <code:table-name/> ADD CHECK (price &gt; 0);
</code:when-checked>
</code:template>

You can read the generated shape directly. <code:columns/> is a hole that the XSLT fills with a list. <code:when-checked> keeps its content only when the table has a check.

The XSLT that fills it¶

The simplest filler is short:

<!-- the values the page needs -->
<xsl:variable name="version" select="(//root-aggregate-version-definition)[1]"/>

<xsl:result-document href="@@page@@hello.html@@" method="html" html-version="5">
    <xsl:apply-templates select="document('templates/page.xml')" mode="page">
        <xsl:with-param name="ctx" tunnel="yes" select="map {
            'counter': string(gal:tagvalue($version, 'counter')),
            'greetings': string(gal:tagvalue($version, 'greetings'))
        }"/>
    </xsl:apply-templates>
</xsl:result-document>

<!-- a code:* mark is replaced by the value of that name -->
<xsl:template match="code:*" mode="page">
    <xsl:param name="ctx" as="map(xs:string, xs:string)" tunnel="yes"/>
    <xsl:value-of select="$ctx(local-name())"/>
</xsl:template>

The idea:

  1. document('templates/page.xml') loads the template. The path is relative to the XSLT folder.
  2. apply-templates walks it. Text and ordinary elements are copied. A code:* element is matched by a template of yours.
  3. The values travel as a map in a tunnel parameter, so every template down the tree can read them.
  4. A mark whose name is a value in the map is replaced. A mark that is a list (like columns) gets a template of its own, which loops over the tags and writes the lines.

gal:ctx($version, ('table-name', 'checked')) builds such a map from the tags of a version. A hyphen in the mark name is an underscore in the tag name.

Why this way¶

  • Readable. The template looks like the output. A person who knows SQL and not XSLT can edit it.
  • Separate. Change the formatting in the template and leave the logic. Change the logic and leave the formatting.
  • Checked. The template is XML, so a missing closing mark is an error when the XSLT loads it.
  • Reusable. The same marks, the same templates, in many generators.

Escaping¶

A template is XML, so <, > and & in the output must be written as &lt;, &gt; and &amp;. Set replace-escaped-form-to-original-symbols to true in the other-files entry for the generated folder, and Galimatron turns them back when it writes the file. The gal.cfg of the messages example does this for its generated source files, and leaves it false for .html and .md.

Note

The code namespace and the mark names are a convention used by the examples. Galimatron does not interpret them. Your XSLT decides what each mark means.

Strings inside tags¶

A string in a tag can also be a template. A string followed by _te replaces {{name}} with the value of the tag name in the same version, when the data is compiled. See Tags. Use _te for a sentence inside the data, and an XML template for a whole file.
